title: Aliasing
body:
Sample too slowly and a high frequency comes back as a low one. It does not come back as noise or
as a distorted version of itself; it comes back as **a different, perfectly clean frequency that
was never there**, and nothing downstream can tell the difference.

Sampling a sine of frequency $f$ at rate $f_s$ produces samples indistinguishable from a sine at
$|f - k f_s|$ for every integer $k$. Once $f > f_s/2$ the smallest of those is below the Nyquist
frequency, and that impostor is what you recorded. Two frequencies that land on the same samples
are called aliases of each other, hence the name.

The familiar cases:

- **The wagon wheel in a film.** 24 frames per second undersamples a spoke rotating faster than 12
  revolutions per second, so the wheel appears to turn slowly backwards.
- **A stroboscope** making a spinning fan look frozen: the strobe rate has aliased the rotation
  down to zero.
- **Moiré patterns** in a photograph of a striped shirt or a brick wall: spatial aliasing, from
  sampling a fine pattern on a coarser pixel grid.

The mechanism, in one line: sampling copies the spectrum every $f_s$ (see [[Sampling Theorem]] and
[[Convolution Theorem]]), and when the copies overlap they add. **The overlap is irreversible.**
The only fix is a low-pass anti-aliasing filter *before* the sampler, which is why every ADC has
one in front of it.

This is the mechanism behind the [[Fidelity]] loss that [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] describes at the
hardware level: raising the [[Sample Rate]] improves fidelity because it raises the Nyquist
frequency and pushes the fold-over point above the content you care about. Undersampled
[[PCM]] audio does not sound quiet or muffled, it sounds *wrong*, and this is why.
